subject: Tyska
title: Grammar: perfect tense
sourceSummary: How the perfect tense is formed with haben or sein, and the most common participle forms.

questions.prompt: How is the perfect tense formed in German?
questions.opener: Two parts: an auxiliary verb and the participle.
choices: Haben or sein conjugated + participle at the end
Only with haben, conjugated at the end
Participle conjugated + haben at the end
questions.explanation: The perfect tense is formed with haben or sein conjugated in position two, and the participle (e.g. gemacht, gefahren) at the end of the sentence: "Ich habe das gemacht."

questions.opener: Regular verbs form the participle with ge- + stem + -t.

questions.prompt: Choose the right auxiliary verb: "Ich ___ nach Berlin gefahren." (fahren = movement)
questions.opener: Verbs that describe movement from one place to another use sein.
questions.explanation: Verbs that describe motion/movement (fahren, gehen, kommen) use "sein" as the auxiliary verb: "ich bin gefahren".

questions.prompt: Choose the right auxiliary verb: "Wir ___ Pizza gegessen." (essen = to eat)
questions.opener: Most verbs that do NOT describe movement use haben.
questions.explanation: "Essen" doesn't describe movement, so it uses "haben": "wir haben ... gegessen".

questions.prompt: Which participle belongs to "sehen" (to see)? An irregular (strong) verb.
questions.opener: Strong verbs form the participle with ge- + (often changed) stem + -en.
questions.explanation: "Sehen" is strong (irregular): participle "gesehen", ending in -en instead of -t.

questions.prompt: Write the participle of "spielen" (to play) — a regular verb.
Correct the error: "Gestern habe ich in die Stadt gegangen." (Yesterday I went to town.)
questions.answer: Gestern bin ich in die Stadt gegangen.
steps: "Gehen" (to go) describes movement, so the auxiliary verb should be "sein", not "haben".
Full sentence: "Gestern bin ich in die Stadt gegangen." (Yesterday I went to town.)

questions.prompt: How is the perfect tense formed in German, and when do you use haben versus sein?
questions.opener: Two auxiliary verbs and two kinds of participles.
questions.answer: Structure: haben/sein conjugated (position 2) + participle (at the end of the sentence). Sein is used for movement/change of state: gehen → ist gegangen, fahren → ist gefahren, kommen → ist gekommen, sein → ist gewesen. Haben is used for most other verbs: machen → hat gemacht, essen → hat gegessen, spielen → hat gespielt, sehen → hat gesehen. Regular participles: ge+stem+t. Strong (irregular) participles: ge+stem+en, often with a changed stem vowel.

questions.prompt: Choose the right auxiliary verb: "Sie ___ nach Hause gekommen." (kommen = movement; she came home)
questions.explanation: "Kommen" describes motion/movement, so it uses "sein": "sie ist ... gekommen".

questions.prompt: Which participle belongs to "trinken" (to drink)? A strong verb.
questions.opener: Strong verbs can change their stem vowel in the participle.
questions.explanation: "Trinken" is strong (irregular): participle "getrunken", with the vowel change i→u.

questions.prompt: Choose the right auxiliary verb: "Wir ___ ins Kino gegangen." (gehen = movement)
questions.explanation: "Gehen" describes motion, so it uses "sein": "wir sind ... gegangen".

questions.prompt: Which participle belongs to "sprechen" (to speak)? A strong verb.
questions.opener: The stem vowel changes from e to o.
questions.explanation: "Sprechen" is strong (irregular): participle "gesprochen", with the vowel change e→o.

questions.prompt: Choose the right auxiliary verb: "Ich ___ müde gewesen." (sein = to be; I was tired)
questions.opener: "Sein" (to be) is one of the verbs that is itself conjugated with sein as its auxiliary.
questions.explanation: "Sein" is conjugated with itself as the auxiliary verb in the perfect tense: "ich bin ... gewesen".

questions.prompt: Which participle belongs to "kaufen" (to buy)? A regular verb.
Which of these verbs describes NO movement and therefore needs haben?
questions.opener: The other three are all classic "sein" verbs.
questions.explanation: "Lesen" (to read) describes no movement, so it uses "haben". "Gehen", "kommen", and "fahren" all describe motion and use "sein".
